items.title: Google DeepMind launches Gemini 4 Neon, a frontier AI model excelling in software engineering, knowledge work, and scientific workflows with a 1 million-token context window [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Introducing Gemini 4 Neon
items.summary:
Google DeepMind introduced Gemini 4 Neon, an advanced AI model designed for fast, end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and scientific workflows. The model ranks highly on multiple AI benchmarks, including #3 overall on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and #2 on the Vals Index, and features improved steerability and reduced fabrication rates. It supports a 1 million-token context window and is priced at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, with a 95% discount on cached inputs.

Gemini 4 Neon integrates multiple input types such as spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video, synthesizing them into structured outputs. It leads in benchmarks related to legal research, tax, finance, accounting, and scientific reasoning, and is optimized for long-running agent workflows and production-ready code, including multi-file debugging and refactoring. The model is available through the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscriptions, supporting enterprise, analytical, and scientific applications.

items.title: Google DeepMind rolls out Genie 4 for Google AI Ultra subscribers, enabling real-time interactive world editing with native audio and a community gallery [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Genie 4 is now available
items.summary:
Google DeepMind has launched Genie 4, its most advanced interactive world model, for eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers. The update allows users to modify virtual environments in real time using natural language prompts, add adaptive native audio, and share creations in a new community gallery. The rollout also includes enhancements to the existing Genie 3 model and introduces a Project Genie agent that assists users in building custom worlds through conversational input.

Genie 4 supports dynamic changes such as weather shifts and character additions during exploration, while Genie 3 offers longer session durations, panorama image grounding, and linked world sequences. The Project Genie agent leverages Google's multimodal models to generate visuals and background scores based on user descriptions, facilitating more complex and immersive world-building experiences. Subscribers can start creating, sharing, and remixing interactive digital worlds directly from their browsers.

items.originalTitle: Gemini 4 Neon looks like an Opus 5.5 competitor
items.summary: Gemini 4 Neon, released with a token processing speed of 127 tokens per second, shows a substantial speed improvement over Gemini 4 Carbon's 46 tokens per second. Modeling suggests Neon’s performance on the Agent Duel leaderboard could be comparable to Opus 5.5, with a projected Elo score close to Opus’s 1,078. The analysis indicates speed is as influential as model identity in determining leaderboard rankings, and Neon is projected to win about 48.3% of matches against Opus 5.5, considering ties as half wins.

items.title: KPMG UK says AI agents asked deeper questions than human auditors in trial examining FTSE 250 company accounts [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI agents ask better questions than KPMG accountants in audit trial
items.summary:
KPMG UK conducted an experiment using over 100 AI agents to audit the financial statements of a major UK-listed FTSE 250 company, finding that the AI sometimes investigated issues more thoroughly and asked better questions than its human audit team. The project, called Project Exponential, involved AI agents performing tasks across the audit process, including data collection, analysis, and drafting conclusions, while working alongside human auditors who maintained oversight.

The trial highlighted both the potential and current limitations of AI in auditing, as human intervention was needed when an AI agent misapplied regulatory requirements. KPMG plans to expand the use of AI agents to larger audits but acknowledges the technology is not yet mature enough for widespread deployment. The experiment raises questions about the future economics and operating models of auditing, though human judgment remains essential for final audit opinions and regulatory compliance.

items.title: Researchers find third-party API routers in coding agents can alter repository actions undetected, undermining client-side safeguards and requiring provider-side integrity guarantees [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Where Is the Cost of Third-Party API Routers in Agentic Software Development?
items.summary:
Researchers conducted an empirical study on the impact of third-party API routers in agentic software development, focusing on their ability to inspect and modify requests between coding agents and upstream providers. They found that these routers, which occupy a trusted path, can inject subtle changes that significantly alter repository-level actions without detection by existing client-side permission mechanisms.

The study introduced SIDEL, a framework for trace recording, replay, injection, and defense evaluation, and tested four coding agents across four levels of router-side injection. Results showed a 0 percent defense success rate without additional mitigations, while client-side controls and reactive reviews improved resistance but failed to fully restore control. The findings highlight the need for provider-side output-integrity guarantees to secure agentic software workflows.
items.description:
Researchers conducted an empirical study on the impact of third-party API routers in agentic software development, focusing on their ability to inspect and modify requests between coding agents and upstream providers. They found that these routers, which occupy a trusted path, can inject subtle changes that significantly alter repository-level actions without detection by existing client-side permission mechanisms.

The study introduced SIDEL, a framework for trace recording, replay, injection, and defense evaluation, and tested four coding agents across four levels of router-side injection. Results showed a 0 percent defense success rate without additional mitigations, while client-side controls and reactive reviews improved resistance but failed to fully restore control. The findings highlight the need for provider-side output-integrity guarantees to secure agentic software workflows.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.23624v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Third-party API routers have become a common layer that unifies access across increasingly diverse LLM providers. In coding-agent workflows, high-autonomy operation is widely adopted because it reduces interaction overhead. As a result, a third-party API router, which sits between the agent and the upstream provider, inevitably occupies the trusted path. It can inspect and modify every request and response, yet no mechanism verifies alignment between the provider's output and the repository-level actions ultimately executed by the agent. Consequently, client-side permission mechanisms may become ineffective in practice. Whether this control gap produces real, hard-to-detect effects on software development tasks remains empirically unmeasured. In this paper, we conduct an empirical study of router-side injection in coding agents, examining four intervention levels of increasing subtlety: Response Substitution (L1), Response Append (L2), LLM-Polished Injection (L3), and LLM-Polished with Distribution Alignment Injection (L4). Moreover, we develop SIDEL, a framework for trace recording, replay, injection, and defense evaluation, with a curated dataset of 400 samples. We evaluate four representative coding agents, and further evaluate whitelist-based execution control and LLM review. Router-side intervention substantially alters repository-level actions and remains difficult for existing client-side safeguards to detect. Without additional mitigations, all evaluated agents achieved a defense success rate of 0 percent across all injection levels. Client-side mitigations and reactive reviews improve resistance but do not fully restore end-to-end control, motivating provider-side output-integrity guarantees. Our code is available at https://github.com/Riyasushin/SIDEL.

They found that these routers, which occupy a trusted path, can inject subtle changes that significantly alter repository-level actions without detection by existing client-side permission mechanisms.

The study introduced SIDEL, a framework for trace recording, replay, injection, and defense evaluation, and tested four coding agents across four levels of router-side injection. Results showed a 0 percent defense success rate without additional mitigations, while client-side controls and reactive reviews improved resistance but failed to fully restore control. The findings highlight the need for provider-side output-integrity guarantees to secure agentic software workflows.

items.title: Researchers introduce RPMem, a model-independent parametric memory architecture for LLM agents that evolves across sessions and transfers across backbone replacements [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: RPMem: Learning Long-Term Recurrent Parametric Memory Across Sessions for LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers present RPMem, a two-stage architecture designed to provide long-term recurrent parametric memory for large language model (LLM) agents that persists and evolves across sessions. RPMem compiles each session into a model-independent latent memory and integrates it with retained memory via a task-trained recurrent gate, then maps the consolidated memory to backbone-specific low-rank adaptation parameters to enable transferability when the backbone model is replaced.

Evaluations on three long-term memory benchmarks and five diverse backbone models demonstrate RPMem's broad generalization with near-constant update cost and memory footprint. Using Qwen3-8B on the PERMA benchmark, RPMem achieved 85.52% accuracy, outperforming the strongest parametric and text-based baselines by 5.32 and 12.98 percentage points respectively. Ablation studies confirm the complementary roles of session compilation and cross-session consolidation, while analysis shows the recurrent gate learns task-specific memory integration strategies. This establishes RPMem as a lifecycle-independent parametric memory framework that maintains evolving cross-session memory reusable across backbone replacements.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.23466v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-running LLM agents require memory that persists and evolves across sessions. Text-based memory retrieves and reconstructs past interactions at every query, making long-horizon performance increasingly dependent on retrieval quality and contextual reasoning as histories grow. Parametric memory encodes experience directly into model computation, but existing approaches provide limited support for cross-session memory evolution. Their coupling to a specific backbone further restricts memory reuse after model replacement. We introduce RPMem, a two-stage architecture that compiles each session into a model-independent latent memory through forward computation and selectively integrates it with retained memory via a task-trained recurrent gate. The consolidated memory is then mapped to backbone-specific low-rank adaptation (LoRA) parameters, allowing the encoding capability to transfer when the backbone is replaced. Evaluation across three long-term memory benchmarks and five diverse backbones demonstrates broad generalization with near-constant update cost and memory footprint. With Qwen3-8B on PERMA, RPMem reaches 85.52%, outperforming the strongest parametric and text-based baselines by 5.32 and 12.98 percentage points, respectively. Ablations validate the complementary roles of session compilation and cross-session consolidation, while dynamics analyses reveal that the gate acquires task-specific memory integration strategies. These results establish RPMem as a lifecycle-independent parametric memory framework that maintains evolving cross-session memory that remains reusable across backbone replacements. Our code is available at https://github.com/Quark-Medical/rpmem/tree/main.

items.originalTitle: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
items.summary: Researchers present Gamer, a generalist agent framework designed for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments, combining perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning in an end-to-end architecture. The model is trained on tens of thousands of hours of keyboard and mouse interaction data spanning simulated games and embodied environments, enabling it to learn dynamics across physical and virtual domains. Gamer uses sparse-thinking instruction tuning to reduce redundant computation and a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method to handle finite context windows, rollout errors, and sparse rewards. A cloud-edge inference engine supports real-time interaction across multiple simulated game environments with low latency. Gamer demonstrates strong generalization and efficiency comparable to skilled players in challenging 3D open-world games and achieves competitive results on conventional 2D game benchmarks, suggesting that scaling data and learning algorithms on repetitive input trajectories can improve complex skill acquisition. This approach offers a pathway toward generalist agents capable of interacting across digital and physical worlds.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.18397v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.

items.title: Researchers audit world-model explanations in retail forecasting, finding models pass trust checks but still misestimate lift and price response, risking costly errors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated world-model and LightGBM forecasting models that explain sales forecasts as a baseline plus lift from price and promotion plans. Despite passing multiple predefined checks for explanation trustworthiness, both models overstate lift by 23% to 42% in simulated store data, leading to significant stock ordering errors. The world model also exaggerated the response to lasting price changes by up to 6.5 times the true effect, revealing that passing explanation sanity checks does not guarantee accuracy about real-world effects.

The study applied eight checks to assess faithfulness, stability, and price direction on generated data with known effects and on nine real datasets. While baseline and lift components summed correctly under each model's plan, deeper price cuts sometimes paradoxically lowered forecasts. Across 703 model configurations, passing explanation checks showed no correlation with actual accuracy. These findings highlight limitations in current explanation methods for retail forecasting models and suggest caution when relying on them for inventory and promotion decisions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.20811v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Forecasting models that read the price and promotion plan explain each forecast as a baseline, what would sell with nothing planned, plus the lift the plan adds, and merchants order stock and plan promotions on that lift. We show that an explanation can pass the checks used to trust it and still be wrong enough to cost money. We define eight checks for any forecaster that states a plan lift, six with a pass rule fixed before any result, and run them on a world model and on LightGBM. In generated store data with known effects, the world model passes the checks of construction, stability, price direction and agreement with sales and with LightGBM, yet when merchants plan into high-demand weeks it states 1.33 to 1.40 times the true lift, and 1.23 to 1.42 times in eight variants of that world; LightGBM overstates it too (1.26, and 1.16 to 1.35). Both still pick the right weeks to promote, but stock ordered to the world model's lift is off by 0.44 to 0.48 of the true lift. The world model's stated response to a lasting regular-price change is 4.7 to 6.5 times the true -0.5, an error in kind that only a measured cause finds. Sanity checks for explanations test whether an explanation depends on the model; a decision needs to know whether it is right about the world, and these results show the first does not give the second. For the final tuned world models of our companion paper on nine data sets, baseline and lift add up under each model's own plan on every window, but a deeper price cut lowers the forecast in 29% to 83% of item-week steps on Dominick's. Across 703 configurations from the settings searches, checks passed were not related to accuracy (Spearman 0.02, 95% interval -0.02 to 0.05). A noisy benchmark of price episodes in Dominick's data is reported as a check of direction only.

items.title: Researchers analyze mechanistic links between in-context learning and out-of-context hallucination in large language models, identifying role span contributions as key factors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Mechanistic Analysis of In-Context Learning and Out-of-Context Hallucination
items.summary:
Large language models can follow specific rules through in-context learning (ICL) but sometimes produce out-of-context (OOC) hallucinations by failing to adhere to provided evidence. This study unifies the understanding of ICL and OOC hallucination by examining the functional roles within dynamic context, showing that internal role representations do not always constrain outputs effectively. The researchers derive a decomposition of role effects, revealing that their influence depends on sufficient contribution magnitude and coherent aggregation, which affect key token choices related to response structure, content, and factual accuracy.

Causal analysis demonstrates that role span contributions are critical for making role-consistent decisions, and failures can be reversed when adequate role support is present. These findings suggest a common mechanistic framework where each functional role shapes output decision patterns, and variations in this organization explain the contrasting outcomes of faithful in-context learning and hallucination.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.24000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models can infer and follow specific rules through in-context learning (ICL), yet may fail to remain faithful to provided evidence, giving rise to out-of-context (OOC) hallucination. Existing work has largely investigated the underlying mechanisms of ICL and OOC hallucination along separate lines. However, this separation obscures the mechanistic basis for these seemingly opposing outcomes. In this work, we study this contrast through the unified view of functional roles in dynamic context. The key observation is that role information can be internally represented without reliably constraining output. We derive a first-order decomposition to characterize the role effect, showing that its substantial influence depends on two necessary conditions, namely sufficient contribution magnitude and coherent signed aggregation. Causal analysis further shows that role span contributions affect key token choices involving response structure, content selection, and factual values. We further show that role-consistent choices depend on sufficient role span support at these key decisions, while failing choices can be reversed when this support overcomes the deficit. These findings support a common mechanistic view of ICL and OOC hallucination: each functional role defines the pattern of output decisions over which role span contributions must remain effective, and differences in this organization account for the seemingly opposing outcomes.

items.title: Researchers introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview, a 35-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 3 billion activated parameters and thinking-mode generation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report
items.summary:
Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover) is a new language model that combines recurrent memory with bidirectional softmax attention to improve generation quality and speed. It achieves leading scores on seven agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and generates text at 680 tokens per second on a single NVIDIA GB300 GPU.

The model uses Gated Delta Networks to manage block diffusion and includes a decision-model variant that answers related questions in one denoising pass, improving question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0% on an internal dataset of 500 groups. Evaluations focus on model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory conditions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.24636v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.

items.title: Study finds continual pre-training benefits Quebec French language models only when base competence is low, with corpus composition more impactful than data volume [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Does Continual Pre-Training Help? A Controlled Study of Dialectal Adaptation for Qu\'ebec French
items.summary: Researchers conducted a controlled study of continual pre-training (CPT) on nine large language models to adapt them to Quebec French, using a fixed budget of 30 million tokens per experiment. They found that CPT's effectiveness depends heavily on the model's initial competence in the dialect, with improvements driven mainly by the type of training data rather than its quantity, particularly literary texts. The study also showed that CPT enhances expression comprehension more than grammatical skills and that the register of the training corpus influences which regional expressions the model learns. Additionally, some capability-specific trade-offs were observed, such as declines in reading comprehension that aggregate evaluation scores may obscure. These results suggest that CPT should not be applied indiscriminately for dialectal adaptation; instead, strategies should start with assessing the base model's existing abilities and include detailed data and task-level evaluations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.24699v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) is widely used to adapt pretrained language models to dialectal and non-standard language varieties, yet it remains unclear when this additional training is necessary, what drives its benefits, and whether aggregate evaluation scores adequately capture its effects. In this paper, we present a controlled study of CPT for Qu\'ebec French language understanding across nine LLMs spanning different families and scales. Using a budget-matched protocol of 30M tokens per experiment, our results show that the benefit of CPT depends strongly on the starting model's existing competence in the target variety. When CPT is beneficial, the improvements are driven more by corpus composition than by data volume, with literary text accounting for most of the gain. Paired Qu\'ebec and standard French evaluations further show that CPT primarily improves expression comprehension rather than grammatical competence, and that corpus register determines which regional expressions are acquired. These gains also involve capability-specific trade-offs, including declines in reading comprehension that aggregate scores can conceal. Overall, these findings show that CPT for dialectal adaptation should not be treated as a uniformly beneficial default. Instead, adaptation strategies should begin with a careful assessment of the base model's existing competence, accompanied by source-level data analysis and task-level evaluation.

items.title: QDA system uses LLM agents to design post-training quantization recipes for large language models, improving accuracy and reducing evaluation time across multiple models and precisions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
items.summary:
QDA introduces an agent-driven approach to optimize post-training quantization recipes for large language models, addressing the challenge of model-specific and precision-specific tuning that is typically time-consuming and sub-optimal. The system accelerates evaluation by scoring candidates based on KL divergence from the original model outputs and verifies promising recipes with longer generation tests to detect failures like repetition loops.

QDA also provides a compatible library of public quantization methods to streamline building and testing across different architectures. It demonstrated accuracy improvements over the strongest existing recipes by up to 2.2 percentage points on various reasoning models and recovered 98.3% of the accuracy of a 320B-parameter MoE model compared to 96.9% from the best vendor checkpoint, all while maintaining compatibility with existing serving kernels and incurring no inference overhead. The authors plan to release the library, evaluator, and harness to the public.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.23388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.

items.title: Researchers propose SpecLook, a training-free speculate-and-verify framework for agentic multimodal large language models that improves speed and accuracy by predicting and verifying next observations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SpecLook: Speculating Where to Look for Fast and Reliable Agentic MLLMs
items.summary:
Researchers introduce SpecLook, a framework designed to accelerate and enhance the reliability of agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that interleave reasoning with image zoom-in tool calls. SpecLook speculates the agent's next observation rather than the answer, allowing verification and correction without running slow sequential loops. The framework uses a small model to draft glimpses and re-answer questions, with a large model verifying and fusing answers only when necessary, significantly reducing computation.

Extensive experiments on datasets including V*, HR-Bench, and POPE demonstrate that SpecLook achieves higher accuracy than existing baselines while providing speedups of up to 9.9 times compared to prior agentic models like DeepEyes-7B and Thyme-RL. The approach also generates reliability scores for answers without requiring labeled data, offering a more efficient and trustworthy method for agentic MLLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.23483v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that think with images interleave reasoning with zoom-in tool calls. However, this sequential loop is slow, and its answers carry no reliability score. Prior speculation of tokens, reasoning steps, or answers keeps the loop, and answer speculation also accepts confident errors. We find that the loop mostly adds one zoom-in step, with which a small model is ahead of the agent on most splits. Our key insight is to speculate the agent's next observation, which, unlike a drafted answer, can be verified, corrected, and used to test the answer. We propose SpecLook, a training-free speculate-and-verify framework with three levels. A small model drafts a glimpse and re-answers from it, and the question ends if the answer is unchanged and confident. Otherwise, the agent's large model verifies and corrects the glimpse without tools, and their answers are fused. Only questions that still lack evidence reach the agent, in one forward pass that SpecLook-Fast skips, so no question runs the loop. The trace scores every answer's reliability without labels. Extensive experiments on V*, HR-Bench, and POPE show that both are more accurate than every baseline on every split. SpecLook reaches 87.2% and 86.2% mean accuracy with 7.7x and 4.7x speedups over the DeepEyes-7B and Thyme-RL agents, and SpecLook-Fast reaches 9.9x and 6.3x.

items.title: Researchers introduce Communicative On-Policy Distillation to improve language-model agents by using natural-language communication to distill black-box teacher capabilities for long-horizon tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Communicative On-Policy Distillation: Distilling Black-Box Teacher Capabilities through Communication for Long-Horizon Tasks
items.summary:
Researchers present Communicative On-Policy Distillation (COPD), a method that enables smaller student language models to learn from stronger black-box teacher models through natural-language communication during task execution. The student autonomously decides when to consult the teacher and formulates open-ended requests without predefined templates, retaining successful interactions to guide self-distillation alongside reinforcement learning.

COPD demonstrated a 2.46-fold improvement over the strongest black-box on-policy distillation baseline on the CAMG-II benchmark. The capabilities learned through this communication-based approach generalized to other benchmarks, including Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, enhancing task success without requiring ongoing adviser access.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.23673v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a powerful paradigm for improving language-model agents on long-horizon tasks, yet its conventional formulation relies on teacher logits that text-only black- box models do not expose. To address this limitation, we introduce Communicative On-Policy Distillation (COPD), which uses natural-language communication as a medium for distilling a stronger model's capabilities into a smaller student. During task execution, the student au- tonomously decides when to consult a black-box teacher and formulates open-ended natural- language requests without predefined question templates or intervention schedules. Successful student-teacher interactions are retained as privileged references to supervise fresh adviser-free student rollouts through on-policy self-distillation, jointly with task-reward reinforcement learning. On CAMG-II, COPD achieves 2.46 times the gain of the strongest black-box OPD baseline. The capabilities it learns through communication generalize to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, improving task success without adviser access.

items.title: Researchers study small language models learning from user feedback with discernment mechanisms, finding improvement followed by decay over a year in 127 live tests [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning through Discernment: when a small language model learns from user feedback on the job, and when it decays
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated small language models (Qwen3 0.6B and 1.7B) fine-tuned nightly using user feedback filtered by different judgment mechanisms over 127 live sessions lasting up to a year. They compared true outcomes, user verdicts, and the model's own judgments with a separate "feedback sense" designed to interpret user reactions, finding that models improved initially but then decayed, especially when feedback was ambiguous or failures were misclassified as successes.

The study showed that a feedback sense discerning clear user verdicts maintained model performance near an oracle for two weeks before fading, while a sense that treated polite user give-ups as successes led to collapse in most cases. When users could not see outcomes, the feedback sense correctly read reactions, but 80% of lessons were failures the user had thanked, indicating misleading feedback. Overall, learning from users was effective only when failures were excluded and users had outcome visibility; otherwise, biased lessons could narrow model capabilities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.23716v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small language models on devices could keep improving by learning, overnight, from their own daily work. Without a true outcome, however, something must decide which attempts are worth learning from, and both the model's own judgment and the user's reaction can be wrong. We study a small model (Qwen3 0.6B and 1.7B) with a LoRA adapter, fine-tuned each night on the attempts a judge accepts, over 127 lives of up to a year on WebShop and $\tau^2$-bench. We compare the true outcome, the user's stated verdict and the model's own judgment with a separate, frozen "feedback sense" that reads the user's reaction, built in three versions. Judging itself, the model improved and then decayed, over a year and whatever its adapter. A sense that took polite give-ups for success collapsed 3 of 5 lives; one built for discernment, which first asks whether the user gave a clear verdict, kept 4 of 5 near the oracle for two weeks, then faded on clean but scarce lessons, to the level of self-judging by day 60. When the user cannot see the outcome ($\tau^2$-bench), the sense read reactions correctly, yet 80% of its lessons were failures the customer had thanked. Across 97 lives, the share of failed attempts among the lessons predicted the outcome (Spearman $\rho$ = -0.81). In our experiments, learning from users held up only where the judge kept failures out and the user could see the outcome; lopsided lessons may also narrow the model.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.23751v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous LLM agents incur substantial cost and latency by invoking a large model (System-2) at every step, even when many intermediate actions choose among a small set of known candidates. Existing dual-system agents offload such decisions to a lightweight System-1 model, but rely on workflow-specific hooks authored per environment. We present AnyS1, a framework that turns human-authored procedural skills, whose instructions naturally specify where choices arise and which options apply, into a shared, domain-general source of decision points. Offline, AnyS1 mines grounded enumerable decisions across over 1,000 public skills, gathers execution-grounded trajectory states inside isolated containers to construct Any-DP, and trains a single calibrated 4B pointer System-1 with label smoothing. At run time, compiled workflows resolve routine decisions in one forward pass and fall back to System-2 when confidence falls below a calibrated threshold. Across three unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families, AnyS1 preserves task reliability while cutting episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent, and maintains performance under zero-shot threshold transfer.

items.title: Researchers find extending fixed-horizon latent Chain-of-Thought reasoning can degrade performance and propose adaptive horizon adjustment to improve accuracy and reduce computation
items.originalTitle: Rethinking Fixed-Horizon Latent Reasoning
items.summary:
Researchers have found that running latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning for a fixed, full preset horizon can degrade reasoning performance, as later stages mainly reorganize existing candidates and may weaken support for correct answers. They propose a lightweight method that estimates remaining reasoning progress and adaptively adjusts the latent horizon during inference, improving reasoning accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points and reducing computation by up to 29% without retraining the language model.

The study characterizes reasoning benefits by realized and remaining constructive progress, showing that higher realized progress correlates with better current accuracy, while more remaining progress indicates potential future gains. Their method was tested across multiple latent CoT reasoners and arithmetic benchmarks, demonstrating consistent improvements in efficiency and accuracy.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.24001v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing latent reasoners typically run for a preset latent horizon during inference. Intuitively, a longer horizon should provide more opportunity for reasoning. However, in this work, we find that extending latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to the full preset horizon may in fact degrade reasoning performance. We observe that latent CoT evolves through distinct functional stages, with earlier computation forming frontier reasoning states, while later computation mainly reorganizes existing candidates and can weaken gold candidate support. These findings motivate a rethink of fixed-horizon latent inference. To address this, we characterize the reasoning benefits of latent CoT by realized and remaining constructive progress. Empirically, we find that higher realized constructive progress corresponds to higher current reasoning accuracy, while more remaining progress corresponds to larger future gains from continued latent CoT. To this end, we introduce a lightweight method that estimates the remaining reasoning progress and adaptively adjusts the latent horizon during inference. Across representative latent CoT reasoners and multiple arithmetic benchmarks, our method improves reasoning accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points while reducing latent computation by up to 29.0%, without retraining the LLM.

items.title: MoE-Context: Show the Model Only What It Needs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MoE-Context: Show the Model Only What It Needs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.24379v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents read their whole history at every step. People do not work like that: we keep what the moment needs and hold the rest as a rough note we can recall. MoE-Context applies this to language models. The context is split into blocks. Before each step a fast yes or no pass decides which blocks the step needs; the rest stay as one-line notes that can be brought back, and nothing is deleted. In the version we build, one model makes this decision and then answers, over a single key-value cache where hidden blocks are masked rather than removed. On a laptop with Qwen3-1.7B and a synthetic lookup task, showing only the needed block raises accuracy from 93 to 119 of 120, and a masked block is as hidden as a deleted one. The model's own picking is the weak part. A supervised linear probe written into spare output rows lifts its accuracy from 80 to 110 of 120, but simple keyword search picks perfectly on this task, and the probe does not transfer to a second task. We report these results openly, along with two cheap usage patterns that block switching enables: undoing a failed attempt and running subagents without a new context.

items.title: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.24711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents that do science must choose informative experiments and reason from their results, but most discovery benchmarks cannot separate that skill from recall, unstated scoring rules or shortcut policies. We introduce Openhagen Worlds, a suite of 27 procedurally generated environments (some with finite truth spaces), from classic puzzles of experimental reasoning to simulator-grounded physics and chemistry, in which an agent runs experiments under a budget and commits an answer that a deterministic verifier checks against a hidden truth. Every observation states the complete scoring rule, and each of the 178 difficulty levels is calibrated: it is admitted only if, on 64 development instances, a scripted oracle succeeds on at least 0.75, the strongest plausible non-deductive policy on at most 0.25 and each gated shortcut on at most 0.35. The 92 core levels span all 27 families and are sized to train small models; the 86 frontier rungs extend the 15 discovery worlds with harder questions and with campaigns of three, five and eight or more committed stages on one hidden system. On the same 84 withheld frontier instances, one per family and rung, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash solves 32 at its default reasoning effort with 16,384 tokens per call and 57 at its maximum effort with up to 393,216 tokens per call (oracle: 79); the headroom that remains is largest in eight-stage campaigns. On-policy expert iteration gives a 9B model modest gains: its core-tier success on trained families rises from 0.090 to 0.148, partly through better action format, with no detectable loss on GPQA Diamond. A hosted service plays the core tier's withheld instances.

items.title: Mixtures of In-Context Learners [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mixtures of In-Context Learners
items.summary: arXiv:2411.02830v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) adapts LLMs by providing demonstrations without fine-tuning the model parameters; however, it does not differentiate between demonstrations and quadratically increases the complexity of Transformer LLMs, exhausting the memory. As a solution, we propose Mixtures of In-Context Learners (MoICL), a novel approach to treat subsets of demonstrations as experts and learn a weighting function to merge their output distributions based on a training set. In our experiments, we show performance improvements on 5 out of 7 classification datasets compared to a set of strong baselines (up to +13\% compared to ICL and LENS). Moreover, we enhance the Pareto frontier of ICL by reducing the inference time needed to achieve the same performance with fewer demonstrations. Finally, MoICL is more robust to out-of-domain (up to +11\%), imbalanced (up to +49\%), or noisy demonstrations (up to +38\%) or can filter these out from datasets. Overall, MoICL is a more expressive approach to learning from demonstrations without exhausting the context window or memory.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning with Reference-Based Rewards for Language Model Reasoning and Alignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reinforcement Learning with Reference-Based Rewards for Language Model Reasoning and Alignment
items.summary: arXiv:2504.09895v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) powers two major lines of large language model (LLM) post-training: reasoning, which elicits deliberate, verifiable problem solving, and alignment, which steers models toward helpful, harmless, and honest behavior. Both hinge on reward design. Reasoning relies on rule-based verification of final answers, whose binary feedback is blind to intermediate derivations, whereas process reward models (PRMs) require step-level annotations too costly to scale. Alignment depends on reward models (RMs) trained on binary preference pairs, making both data collection and model training resource-intensive. We propose RL2R, reinforcement learning with reference-based rewards, as a unified and inexpensive alternative. Using pre-existing or distilled references, RL2R measures semantic similarity with lightweight metrics such as BERTScore between a sampled generation and a reference answer or solution. Similarity preserves ordinal quality signals that binary feedback discards: responses closer to the reference earn higher rewards, and sound derivations receive credit even when the final conclusion is wrong. For mathematical reasoning, augmenting rule-based verification with answer- and step-level similarity provides low-cost process supervision and outperforms answer-only verification. For alignment, a critic-free REINFORCE-style instantiation covers general preference, safety, and confidence tasks on par with RM-based methods. Reference-based rewards thus offer a cost-effective, versatile reward source spanning reasoning and alignment.

items.title: Knowledge Localization in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs Using Cross-Lingual Inconsistency [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Knowledge Localization in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs Using Cross-Lingual Inconsistency
items.summary: arXiv:2603.17102v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern LLMs continue to exhibit significant variance in behavior across languages, such as being able to recall factual information in some languages but not others. While typically studied as a problem to be mitigated, in this work, we propose leveraging this cross-lingual inconsistency as a tool for interpretability in mixture-of-experts (MoE) LLMs. Our knowledge localization framework contrasts routing for sets of languages where the model correctly recalls information from languages where it fails. This allows us to isolate model components that play a functional role in answering about a piece of knowledge. Our method proceeds in two stages: (1) querying the model with difficult factual questions across a diverse set of languages to generate "success" and "failure" activation buckets and then (2) applying a statistical contrastive analysis to the MoE router logits to identify experts important for knowledge. To validate the necessity of this small number of experts for answering a knowledge question, we deactivate them and re-ask the question. We find that despite only deactivating about 20 out of 6000 experts, the model no longer answers correctly in over 40% of cases. Generally, this method provides a realistic and scalable knowledge localization approach to address increasingly complex LLMs.

items.title: HYPER: Hypothesis-Guided Planning for Evidence-Seeking Retrieval [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: HYPER: Hypothesis-Guided Planning for Evidence-Seeking Retrieval
items.summary: arXiv:2603.19008v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves Large Language Models (LLMs) by grounding generation in external, non-parametric knowledge. However, when a task requires choosing among competing possibilities, such as a diagnosis among plausible alternatives, topically relevant context is often insufficient to drive the final decision. To address this issue, we propose HYPER: Hypothesis-Guided Planning for Evidence-Seeking Retrieval, a training-free pre-retrieval planning framework that reorients RAG from topic-oriented retrieval to evidence-oriented retrieval. HYPER uses a provisional answer hypothesis as a planning anchor. It then decomposes retrieval into three evidence roles. Support seeks evidence for the provisional answer. Distinction retrieves criteria that separate competing alternatives. Feature grounds salient question features needed for the decision. This planning step steers retrieval toward evidence near the decision boundary, enabling the generator to answer from context that is more directly aligned with the required choice. On MedQA and MMLU-Med, where single-query retrieval falls below no-retrieval chain-of-thought prompting, HYPER achieves the best average accuracy among ten baselines, improving over Simple RAG by 5.9 and 3.6 points, respectively. Its gains transfer to the 14 subjects of MMLU-Pro, at the cost of two additional LLM calls per question. Code is available at https://github.com/hangeol/HypothesisRAG.

items.title: Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Language Models via Infilling [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Language Models via Infilling
items.summary: arXiv:2605.24173v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Memorization in large language models has been studied almost exclusively through prefix-conditioned extraction, a natural choice for autoregressive models. However, diffusion language models (DLMs) can denoise masked tokens at arbitrary positions. Thus, prefix-only probing reveals only one facet of memorization in DLMs and significantly underestimates the risk of training-data extraction. In order to realistically model extractability of training data in DLMs, we introduce infilling extraction, a data-extraction protocol parameterized by an arbitrary binary mask that subsumes prefix-only probing and accounts for the bidirectional inductive bias of DLMs. Instantiating it on LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B across five extraction modes, three training pipelines, and three corpora covering verbatim and partial leakage, we find that mask geometry governs extractability: edge-conditioned masks extract up to three times more verbatim sequences than prefix-conditioned ones, and bidirectional access opens channels inaccessible in autoregressive models. In particular, an adversary who obtains a PII-redacted copy of the training data can use targeted infilling to raise PII recall on fine-tuned DLMs by 2.5-4.5x over prefix-conditioned extraction, substantially narrowing the gap to a scale-matched autoregressive model and, for LLaDA on email addresses, exceeding it under greedy prefix-conditioned extraction. Tunable parameters for decoding measurably affect extraction performance, while a follow-up supervised fine-tuning stage does not eliminate the prior memorization.

items.title: Multimodal Information Fusion for Chart Understanding: A Survey of MLLMs -- Evolution, Limitations, and Cognitive Enhancement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Multimodal Information Fusion for Chart Understanding: A Survey of MLLMs -- Evolution, Limitations, and Cognitive Enhancement
items.summary: arXiv:2602.10138v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Chart understanding is a quintessential information fusion task, requiring the seamless integration of graphical and textual data to extract meaning. The advent of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has revolutionized this domain, yet the landscape of MLLM-based chart analysis remains fragmented and lacks systematic organization. This survey provides a comprehensive roadmap of this nascent frontier by structuring the domain's core components. We begin by analyzing the fundamental challenges of fusing visual and linguistic information in charts. We then categorize downstream tasks and datasets, introducing a novel taxonomy of canonical and non-canonical benchmarks to highlight the field's expanding scope. Subsequently, we present a comprehensive evolution of methodologies, tracing the progression from classic deep learning techniques to state-of-the-art MLLM paradigms that leverage sophisticated fusion strategies. By critically examining the limitations of current models, particularly their perceptual and reasoning deficits, we identify promising future directions, including advanced alignment techniques and reinforcement learning for cognitive enhancement. This survey aims to equip researchers and practitioners with a structured understanding of how MLLMs are transforming chart information fusion and to catalyze progress toward more robust and reliable systems.

items.title: When Does Learning to Stop Help? Configuring Risk-Controlled Early Exit for Reasoning-Model Services [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: When Does Learning to Stop Help? Configuring Risk-Controlled Early Exit for Reasoning-Model Services
items.summary: arXiv:2606.30852v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Early exit lowers the cost of serving a reasoning model by stopping its reasoning once a provisional answer looks final. An operator must choose between a learned stopping rule and one static token budget, and savings against full reasoning do not settle the choice. We present a procedure that decides on calibration data from the workload. It certifies both families with Learn-then-Test to one bound on the fraction of all questions that full reasoning answers correctly but early exit does not, prices provisional answers as the serving stack does, and deploys the cheapest certified candidate. Across four models and five benchmarks neither family is better throughout. At a 5% risk target the learned rule saves 10.4-17.0 percentage points more tokens than the static budget on free-form mathematics with Qwen3, with accuracy 2.4-2.9 points below full reasoning, and less on MMLU-Pro on average. Which family costs less also changes with the risk target, in 8 of 15 settings, and with the price of a provisional answer. Across three prices, committing to one family in advance gives up as much as 27.4 points on some workload, whereas selecting on calibration data falls at most 11.6 points short of the better family, on a task with only 99 calibration questions. In a vLLM engine with Qwen3-8B, mean response time fell in proportion to generated tokens. Policies served on a task other than their calibration task exceeded the risk target in 18 of 44 task pairs; recalibration on the new task restored risk control.

items.title: OracleZoom: Reference-Constrained Recursive Image Super-Resolution Beyond Ground Truth [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OracleZoom: Reference-Constrained Recursive Image Super-Resolution Beyond Ground Truth
items.summary: arXiv:2609.06490v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recursive image Super-Resolution (SR) reaches extreme magnification by feeding each prediction back into the same model, like zooming into an image again and again. Real ground truth for deep zooms is impractical to capture (a full $256\times$ target would be a 52 GB image), so predictions at deeper zooms have no supervision. Yet the last ground-truth image still contains the region that every deeper zoom magnifies. OracleZoom turns this region into a training signal. Inspired by on-policy self-distillation, the model trains on its own prediction for one recursive step ($4\times \rightarrow 16\times$), and a cross-scale loss projects each $16\times$ prediction back to the last ground truth at $4\times$. This projection can verify only coarse content, so a no-reference quality objective guides the remaining fine detail, and a latent prior stops this objective from adding hallucinated artifacts. On seven datasets, OracleZoom achieves the highest CLIPIQA at every zoom depth (mean 0.713 vs. 0.621 for Chain-of-Zoom), with the largest gains at the deepest zooms, even though training stops at $16\times$ and optimizes a different quality metric. Pooled over two ground-truth-anchored judges, this added detail comes at the same hallucination rate as Chain-of-Zoom at $16\times$ and a lower rate at $4\times$, and removing the cross-scale loss raises hallucination at $16\times$.
items.description: arXiv:2609.06490v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recursive image Super-Resolution (SR) reaches extreme magnification by feeding each prediction back into the same model, like zooming into an image again and again. This projection can verify only coarse content, so a no-reference quality objective guides the remaining fine detail, and a latent prior stops this objective from adding hallucinated artifacts. On seven datasets, OracleZoom achieves the highest CLIPIQA at every zoom depth (mean 0.713 vs. 0.621 for Chain-of-Zoom), with the largest gains at the deepest zooms, even though training stops at $16\times$ and optimizes a different quality metric. items.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21885v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training.

items.title: A Hybrid Exact-Heuristic Solver for the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation Problem [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Hybrid Exact-Heuristic Solver for the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation Problem
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22043v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We describe the solver we submitted to the second round of the SOICT 2026 contest on the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation problem, a selective pickup-and-delivery routing problem with time windows, open routes and heterogeneous taxis. The solver is a single-file, standard-library Python program that combines (i) a constant-time insertion test based on latest-arrival slack, (ii) greedy insertion, local search and an Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (ALNS) with simulated-annealing acceptance, and (iii) an exact route-selection engine that enumerates, for every taxi, the best feasible route for each request set and then solves the resulting set-packing problem by branch-and-bound strengthened with route-based large neighborhood search, Lagrangian bounds and reduced-cost fixing. The engine is chosen automatically from the instance size, and an independent verifier and a watchdog guarantee that a valid answer is always printed. On the official evaluation (38 scored instances, 5-minute limit) the solver obtained a total benefit of 487,237, finished every run within 277 s and used at most 279 MB; 28 of the 38 instances terminated well before the limit.

items.title: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22245v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.

items.title: HealthCLBench:Evaluating Context Learning in Health Conversations through Controlled Case Clusters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: HealthCLBench:Evaluating Context Learning in Health Conversations through Controlled Case Clusters
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22362v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Complex health conversations require answers grounded in individual information and currently valid evidence. We evaluate health context learning: acquiring, integrating, and applying relevant context during inference with fixed model parameters to answer health questions and respond appropriately to changes in facts, evidence, or task goals. To our knowledge, Chinese-language medical benchmarks have yet to systematically combine explicit contextual difficulties, controlled case variations, and member-specific medical criteria for open-ended answers. We introduce HealthCLBench, comprising 328 controlled clusters, 1,103 cases, and 4,931 rubric criteria across medical consultation and everyday health management. Members share backgrounds while evidence, patient states, or task goals change; each has its own medical scoring requirements. A 70-person medical team annotates and reviews the simulated cases and their rubrics. Human review of 700 full-context responses from the original evaluation yields 90.5% pooled agreement with the original automated judgments at the rubric-item level. We report full-context and query-only results for seven general-purpose models and Ant Afu. Across the eight systems, scores with full context are 11.83 to 31.76 case points and 10.87 to 38.97 geometric cluster points higher than those with the current question alone. GPT-6 Astra leads both full-context metrics at 75.03 and 60.42, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 and Ant Afu. Cross-condition differences describe score changes under the reported evaluation settings. Response comparisons reveal failures in checking historical information, expressing uncertainty when warranted, and ensuring recommendations respect required conditions. The resource supports model comparison and targeted follow-up evaluation.

items.title: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22432v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.

Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. items.originalTitle: CADMAGEDDON: High-Fidelity CAD Reconstruction with Local Inference
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22563v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. For individuals and small companies, bringing this work in-house also requires computational resources they can afford. We introduce CADMAGEDDON, an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD from meshes and can run locally on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops. The method decomposes this complex task into a chain of simple visual decisions about what to construct and what to correct. Geometric tools support precise construction, allowing the agent to focus on visual reasoning. Using the mid-sized Qwen3.8-27B model, CADMAGEDDON outperforms prior approaches, including systems based on frontier models, in reconstruction quality on all the main benchmarks. CADMAGEDDON integrates with FreeCAD, bringing its reconstructions into practitioners' existing CAD workflows. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/cadmageddon

items.title: MillBill: A Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MillBill: A Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22565v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Turning a CAD model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and geometric precision. Language models can generate such workflows by writing geometry and toolpath code for each part, but this makes numerical execution part of the model's task. We introduce MillBill, an agent that separates machining decisions from their geometric execution and verification. Given a boundary-representation part, stock, and material, a locally hosted, mid-sized open model proposes operations and cutting parameters for indexed three-axis machining. A geometric harness generates toolpaths, simulates material removal, and returns feedback for plan refinement. Setup planning accounts for what the available cutters can physically reach, rather than visibility alone. We evaluate the resulting programs by the fraction of the target surface area within the specified tolerance after simulated machining. With Qwen3.8-27B, MillBill outperforms frontier-model approaches that construct their own geometry and toolpath workflows on the evaluated machining tasks. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/millbill

items.title: Born for the Task: Rethinking Quantum Chemistry with Foresighted Agentic Computing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Born for the Task: Rethinking Quantum Chemistry with Foresighted Agentic Computing
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22897v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum chemistry relies on general-purpose software, whose generality leaves many large-scale calculations beyond practical resource budgets. Coding agents make task-specific programs cheap to write, but not efficient ones easy to find: whether a computational strategy is accurate and fast enough becomes clear only after it actually runs at the target scale. We introduce MakoBORN, a foresighted agentic computing framework that synthesizes high performance quantum chemistry programs on demand. MakoBORN anticipates the behavior of each strategy before execution, extrapolating its error from representative small systems and predicting its runtime from the target-scale workload and measured hardware throughputs. Building on these predictions, MakoBORN unfolds the preset schemes of existing packages into independently configurable algorithmic components, selects the fastest strategy within the error tolerance from the predicted accuracy-runtime Pareto frontier, and guides coding agents to compile it with component-level performance predictions. For a Hartree-Fock calculation with 50,024 basis functions, MakoBORN finishes in 1.41 h on a single CPU node, 77$\times$ faster than the estimated runtime of a general-purpose baseline and still 9.8$\times$ faster with development time included. On a single GPU, MakoBORN completes the ubiquitin calculation in 2.1 h, the same order of runtime as the GPU-accelerated package Mako on 64 GPUs, and shortens the B-DNA duplex calculation from an estimated two months to 8.1 h (173$\times$).

items.title: Anticipating or Speculating? Making Futures Pay in AI Ethics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Anticipating or Speculating? Making Futures Pay in AI Ethics
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22268v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Philosophers have recently been trying to develop uniform decision rules for instances in which physicians' judgments diverge from the recommendations of medical artificial intelligence (AI) systems. I argue that this effort is fatally flawed because the performance and appropriate use of algorithmic recommendation systems by physicians are highly context-specific, empirical medical matters rather than epistemological ones. In such instances, general decision rules can be stipulated only to the extent that they abstract away from relevant, indeed determinative, contextual circumstances. The alleged problem of physician-AI disagreement, and others like it, play into longstanding disputes in technology ethics about the viability and utility of envisioning possible futures: is this useful "anticipation" or wasteful "speculation"? I suggest that the two may be distinguished. Anticipation explores plausible futures to help inform present actions under irreducible uncertainty. Speculation abstracts away uncertainty, developing formal solutions to stipulated circumstances whose relationship to the real present is often quite unclear. Efforts to develop crisp philosophical solutions to physician-AI disagreement, among other problems, fall into the latter category. Technology ethics should remember that fruitful futures thinking must both begin from and return to the messy, uncertain present.

items.title: MAVE: Reconstructing Editable 3D Blockouts from Film Shots [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MAVE: Reconstructing Editable 3D Blockouts from Film Shots
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22464v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Animated 3D blockouts support previsualization and provide structural conditions for video generation, but manually reconstructing them from reference videos is costly. This limits both their use by creators and the production of paired training data. We introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark of 50 film shots and 416 keyframes for evaluating camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking. We propose MAVE, a video-to-blockout framework combining Metric observation, Agentic modeling, and evidence-based VErification. It first recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system. An agent then constructs an editable environment under constraints from these observations, while programmatic checks report inconsistencies to guide refinement. The outputs are editable Blender scenes and frame-aligned blockout videos. On MAVEBench, MAVE improves overall scores by 27.5-41.1 points across three agents over their corresponding vanilla baselines. With DeepSeek-1017, it achieves a score of 73.2 at an average API cost of only USD 0.054 per shot, outperforming the strongest vanilla baseline while reducing total reconstruction time by 53%. We also construct MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout-video pairs for model training, and will release it publicly. Creators can change viewpoints and character paths, then render the edited scenes to condition video generation. Code is available at https://github.com/yfChang-cv/MAVE.

items.title: Hierarchical Control of Antiphase Synchronization in Biomorphic Spiking Neural Architectures for Locomotor Control [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Hierarchical Control of Antiphase Synchronization in Biomorphic Spiking Neural Architectures for Locomotor Control
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22639v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Central pattern generators (CPGs) provide a biologically inspired foundation for adaptive locomotor control, yet systematically characterizing their dynamic regimes in spiking neural networks remains challenging. This study introduces a framework for identifying and stabilizing antiphase synchronization in a biomorphic spiking CPG model embedded in a closed neuromuscular loop. A composite synchronization metric is developed, integrating phase coherence, amplitude balance, and temporal stability. Its performance is evaluated across systematically varied stimulation waveforms and synaptic configurations. Statistical analysis reveals that stimulation type dominates regime determination, with tonic drive yielding the most robust antiphase synchronization. Periodic inputs induce nonlinear saturation and context-dependent network routing. Although synaptic weights alone show limited discriminative power, they significantly modulate robustness within a given stimulation context, with reciprocal Ia interneuron connections emerging as key stabilizers. The proposed composite metric achieves robust antiphase detection, outperforming traditional phase-only measures while preserving biophysical interpretability. These findings establish a statistically validated, hierarchical modeling approach in which external drive defines the operating regime and targeted synaptic configurations fine-tune dynamic stability, providing actionable guidelines for closed-loop neuromechanical controllers and adaptive neuroprosthetic interfaces.

items.title: Check Your Blind Spots: Decision-Guided Perception by Probing the Planner with Hypothetical Objects [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Check Your Blind Spots: Decision-Guided Perception by Probing the Planner with Hypothetical Objects
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23030v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Not every perception error changes the planner's action. Yet adaptive-resolution perception chooses where to spend high-resolution computation from image cues, which can neither reliably point to an object that low resolution missed nor tell which objects matter to the planner. We observe that the planner can say where an object would matter before anything is seen: inserting a hypothetical object at a location tests whether its action would change. Decision-Guided Speculative Perception (DGSP) treats the low-resolution scene and its action as a draft and probes the planner in this way to obtain a decision-sensitivity field, the locations where an unseen object would change the action. Only this field and the support, the detections on which the current action rests, are verified at high resolution, repeatedly until the action is stable. For two planner classes, we prove that DGSP returns exactly the action of whole-frame high-resolution perception if crop detections match whole-frame ones and the crops cover the field, conditions that real images meet approximately. On three driving datasets, it reproduces this action on about 98% of frames with about a quarter of the pixels. At the pixel cost of uniform downscaling, it repairs more of the draft's disagreements with this action, brakes falsely less often, and recovers many more of the decision-relevant objects that the draft misses.
